title: A Density-Matrix Framework for Electronic-Structure Analysis of Functional-Group and Salt Effects in Lithium-Metal Electrolytes

images.desc:
The EMolStudio Platform


EMolStudio is an electronic-structure analysis workflow for studying electrolyte chemistry at library scale, linking molecular design to solvation, desolvation, and interphase reactivity in lithium-metal electrolytes. The density matrix serves as its common representation for analyzing frontier orbitals (HOMO and LUMO), ESP, dipole moments, Li+–donor bond order, orbital-fragment localization, and Li+-centered ELF deformation descriptors.


EMolStudio combines input definition, structure generation, density-matrix prediction, electronic-structure postprocessing, and interactive organization. The input layer accepts user instructions, Cartesian coordinates, and simplified molecular-input line-entry system (SMILES) strings to define molecules, salts, and local solvation environments. EMolConf constructs functionalized molecules, assembles explicit Li+ first-shell clusters, and relaxes their geometries; EMolES learns the relation between relaxed structures and density matrices; EMolPipe converts density matrices into scalar properties and spatial electronic-structure objects; and EMolAgent, a language-model copilot, maps design questions to structured tasks and organizes interactive result views.


Figure 1: EMolStudio workflow for molecular functionalization and solvation electronic-structure analysis. From user instructions, Cartesian coordinates, or SMILES strings, EMolConf builds functionalized molecules and explicit Li+ first-shell clusters and relaxes their geometries. EMolES predicts the density matrix of each relaxed structure as a shared representation for downstream analysis, EMolPipe parses it into scalar descriptors and spatial visualization objects, and EMolAgent maps user questions to design tasks and organizes the resulting analysis views. Outputs combine scalar properties with frontier-orbital isosurfaces, ESP-mapped surfaces, and Li+-centered ELF deformation descriptors.


Figure 1 summarizes this modular workflow, in which the same descriptor definitions are carried from molecular functionalization to local solvation-shell analysis.


EMolConf Structure Generation


EMolConf is the structure-generation layer of EMolStudio, converting functional-group edits and Li+ first-shell compositions into relaxed three-dimensional structures through a shared geometry-preparation and relaxation workflow based on the Universal Models for Atoms (UMA) potential[31], so that molecular and cluster analyses rest on a common structural basis.


To preserve the parent molecular configuration by construction, molecular functionalization is implemented as a rigid-body fragment attachment. Each functional group is stored as a three-dimensional template whose terminal marker atom defines its bonding vector, and attachment aligns this vector antiparallel to the parent C–H axis at a covalent-radius-derived bond length. A torsional scan about the nascent bond then selects a sterically clash-free rotamer, and valence checks with layer-wise International Chemical Identifier (InChI) deduplication keep the products unique and chemically valid through exact-depth enumeration of up to four functionalization steps per scaffold.


For Li+ first-shell cluster construction, EMolConf reads solvents, lithium-salt anions, and local compositions from the Agent-Translated Design Space produced by EMolAgent and generates initial local structures following the assembly sequence in Figure 2. Lewis-basic site mapping first identifies coordination ends that may face Li+, including carbonyl, ether, and sulfonyl oxygen, nitrile nitrogen, and fluorine. Initial coordination directions are then placed quasi-uniformly around Li+ using a Fibonacci sphere, and shell distances are adjusted according to fragment volume to reduce initial overlap when several fragments enter the first shell. Fragment orientations are further refined by constrained rotational sampling so that donor ends maintain reasonable Li+ contact directions. For sterically congested combinations, adaptive shell expansion increases the shell radius and repeats geometry checks until a relaxable local cluster candidate is obtained. Each assembled cluster additionally carries a dielectric constant, assigned by similarity matching to a curated 72-solvent library with composition weighting or fixed to a user-specified value, which sets the implicit-solvation environment of all downstream cluster calculations (Supporting Information, Section S1.2). The same scaffold–functional-group combination or the same Li+ first-shell composition can generate multiple initial structures to cover different local orientations and metastable coordination arrangements. After UMA relaxation, structures with the same chemical composition are ranked by relative energy, and the relaxed structures are then passed to EMolES density-matrix inference and EMolPipe electronic-structure parsing.


Figure 2: EMolConf chemistry-guided assembly of Li+ first-shell clusters. The Agent-Translated Design Space specifies the salt environment, solvent composition, and anion-excluded, single-anion-contact, or multianion-contact motif; the examples use ethylene carbonate (EC), 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME), and bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (FSI-). Lewis-basic-site mapping identifies donor directions, Fibonacci-sphere seeding distributes candidate contacts around Li+, and volume-aware packing detects steric clashes. Constrained rotational sampling and adaptive shell expansion reduce steric strain before relaxation with the Universal Models for Atoms potential. Atom colors in this and all subsequent atomistic renderings: Li light green, C brown, O red, H white, N blue, S yellow, F pale blue, B pink.


Using this workflow, we constructed an in-house electrolyte electronic-structure dataset for model development. The molecular subset starts from 1,399 electrolyte-solvent parent molecules[18] and applies eight functional groups–methyl (Me), cyano (CN), trifluoromethyl (CF3), fluoro (F), methoxy (OMe), methoxycarbonyl (CO2Me), methylsulfonyl (SO2Me), and fluorosulfonyl (SO2F)–yielding 10,887 molecular structures after functionalization and Li+ coordination-geometry generation. The cluster subset contains 7,200 Li+ first-shell structures covering 72 common solvents and 10 lithium salts, spanning anion-excluded, single-anion-contact, and multianion-contact coordination. Representative outputs of molecular functionalization and cluster assembly are shown in Figures S1 and S2 of the Supporting Information; data generation, filtering, relaxation, and quantum-chemical settings are detailed in Section S1.



EMolES Density-Matrix Model


After relaxed molecular and/or cluster structures are obtained, EMolES uses the density matrix as the central electronic-structure representation of the EMolStudio platform. The density matrix provides a common theoretical basis for frontier orbitals, spatial ESP, dipole moments, local charges, and the Li+-centered ELF deformation factor, allowing these downstream descriptors to be derived consistently[32, 33].


For density-matrix prediction, EMolES is built on the deep-learning tight-binding (DeePTB) framework[34] and its local equivariant representations of quantum operators[29], uses SO(2) tensor-product operations inspired by the Equivariant Spherical Channel Network (eSCN)[35], and introduces an electrostatic-aware message-passing (EAMP) module. EAMP applies keep-in-frame SO(2) tensor-product processing: after edge representations are transformed into a bond-aligned local coordinate frame, they remain in the same local reference frame during subsequent message passing and output preprocessing. Keeping edge features in this frame reduces repeated rotations and preserves edge-level electronic-structure information in high-order orbital channels. Because the density matrix is naturally blocked by atom pairs and orbital pairs, EMolES moves high-order equivariant self-interaction from the node level to atom-pair and orbital-pair edges, following the higher-body-order motivation of MACE[36]. We refer to this edge-wise tensor-product self-mixing module as EACE, or edge-wise atomic cluster expansion. Before node aggregation, it represents directional charge rearrangement in local coordination environments such as Li+–donor and anion–solvent contacts. To balance expressivity and computational cost, this module uses channel-wise tensor products with a uvu connection format and OpenEquivariance acceleration[37]. At the output end, the element-conditioned tensor-product layer modulates orbital-channel coupling according to atomic element and bond-type scalars, followed by fully connected tensor-product channel mixing before output. This design accommodates element-dependent differences in local charge distributions across multielement chemical environments.


Figure 3: EMolES density-matrix architecture and frontier-orbital readout. (a) A three-dimensional atomic graph is encoded by an EAMP backbone with bond-aligned SO(2) message passing, EACE edge-wise self-mix, and an element-conditioned tensor-product layer before density-matrix output. (b) The SO(2) block evaluates edge messages in a bond-local frame. (c) The self-mix block applies channel-wise tensor products to edge features. (d) Comparison between DFT and EMolES-i HOMO/LUMO isosurfaces for the Li1(DFTFB)1(FEC)1(DEC)2 first-shell cluster, with the dominant fragment contribution reported as orbital-component percentage.


The raw EMolES prediction does not exactly conserve electron number or satisfy the closed-shell idempotency constraint. Larger predicted electron-number error (PENE) is associated with larger downstream HOMO/LUMO energy, ESP, and dipole errors (Supporting Information, Figure S3). Accordingly, we introduce an idempotency-projected variant, EMolES-i, as a constrained postprocessing step for closed-shell systems, where “i” denotes idempotent. Specifically, for the density matrix Dμ​νpredD^{\mathrm{pred}}_{\mu\nu} predicted by EMolES and AO overlap matrix Sμ​νS_{\mu\nu}, symmetric orthogonalization gives




D~pred=S1/2​Dpred​S1/2.\tilde{D}^{\mathrm{pred}}=S^{1/2}D^{\mathrm{pred}}S^{1/2}.

(1)


The density matrix in the orthonormal basis is then diagonalized in the natural-orbital basis:




D~pred​U=U​n,\tilde{D}^{\mathrm{pred}}U=Un,

(2)


where UU is the natural-orbital coefficient matrix and nn contains the predicted natural occupations. For a closed-shell system whose total electron number NeN_{\mathrm{e}} is determined by chemical composition, the projected occupations are




niproj={2,i≤Ne/2,0,i>Ne/2.n_{i}^{\mathrm{proj}}=\begin{cases}2,&i\leq N_{\mathrm{e}}/2,\\
0,&i>N_{\mathrm{e}}/2.\end{cases}

(3)


This gives the projected density matrix in the orthonormal basis,




D~proj=U​nproj​UT.\tilde{D}^{\mathrm{proj}}=Un^{\mathrm{proj}}U^{\mathrm{T}}.

(4)


Finally, the matrix is transformed back to the nonorthogonal AO basis:




Dproj=S−1/2​D~proj​S−1/2.D^{\mathrm{proj}}=S^{-1/2}\tilde{D}^{\mathrm{proj}}S^{-1/2}.

(5)


The projected density matrix DprojD^{\mathrm{proj}}, which defines EMolES-i and is used for all analyses in this work, therefore satisfies electron-number conservation and the closed-shell idempotency constraint,




Tr​(Dproj​S)=Ne,Dproj​S​Dproj=2​Dproj.\mathrm{Tr}(D^{\mathrm{proj}}S)=N_{\mathrm{e}},\qquad D^{\mathrm{proj}}SD^{\mathrm{proj}}=2D^{\mathrm{proj}}.

On the in-house molecule and cluster test sets, EMolES and EMolES-i are quantitatively compared with LEM, SLEM, and QHNet[29, 27] (Table 1); test-set construction and evaluation protocols are detailed in Sections S1 and S3 of the Supporting Information. Alongside the density-matrix MAE, the comparison covers frontier-orbital energies and orbital-coefficient similarities, dipole moments and ESP extrema, and two Li+-centered descriptors of the local coordination environment: the ELF deformation factor and average Li+–donor bond order. The unprojected EMolES model gives the lowest density-matrix MAE on both test sets and the lowest reported errors among the unprojected models across the cluster-set properties. After idempotency projection, EMolES-i further reduces most property errors and gives the lowest reported errors on the cluster test set. On the recomputed QH9 labels, idempotency projection similarly reduces the density-matrix-derived property errors (Supporting Information, Tables S4 and S5). These results support the use of edge-level density-matrix learning and idempotency projection for the downstream analyses reported here.

As an out-of-training-set case study, we examine a literature-reported first-shell cluster, Li1(DFTFB)1(FEC)1(DEC)2, in which fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) and diethyl carbonate (DEC) coordinate Li+ together with the DFTFB- anion[38]. This lithium-salt environment is absent from the model training set. The frontier-orbital isosurface topology and fragment-component percentages reconstructed by EMolES-i agree with the DFT dominant-fragment assignments: the HOMO is mainly distributed on the DFTFB- fragment, with a contribution of 99.1%99.1\%, while the LUMO is mainly distributed on the FEC fragment, with a contribution of 96.7%96.7\%. This agreement supports fragment-resolved orbital analysis for this cluster.


We also follow Li+ ligand exchange along a two-stage coordination path in which an entering donor joins the first shell while a leaving donor departs (Supporting Information, Section S4). EMolES-i resolves the relative Li+ binding energy and accompanying Li–O bond-order evolution over the full 1000-frame path, using 30 DFT frames for validation. At those frames, the binding-energy mean absolute error is 0.084 eV (r=0.995r=0.995), compared with 0.380 eV for UMA under the same reference convention. The coupled energy and bond-order profiles place the strongest Li+ binding near transient coordination-shell closure and provide a continuous view between the DFT validation frames.



EMolPipe Electronic-Structure Readouts


EMolPipe is the electronic-structure postprocessing and property-parsing layer of EMolStudio. It links relaxed geometries, predicted density matrices, and spatial grids, converting model outputs into quantitative electronic-structure readouts with provenance; its electronic-structure and wavefunction-analysis routines build on PySCF[39, 40] and Multiwfn[41].


The resulting outputs fall into two categories. Scalar descriptors describe the local chemical environment, including HOMO/LUMO energies, gap, dipole moment, ESP extrema, Li+–donor bond order, Li+-centered ELF deformation factor, and fragment-resolved orbital weights. Spatial electronic-structure objects include HOMO/LUMO isosurfaces, ESP-mapped surfaces, and localized ELF distributions, which are used to analyze frontier-orbital distribution across coordination fragments and to inspect electronic polarization around Li+.


For large molecular and cluster libraries, EMolPipe exports files compatible with the Visualization for Electronic and Structural Analysis (VESTA)[42] and Visual Molecular Dynamics (VMD)[43] programs and parallelizes descriptor extraction through the Portable Batch System (PBS) or DPDispatcher[44]. Each output retains provenance links among the structure, density matrix, wavefunction file, cube file, and parsed descriptor, enabling aggregation by parent scaffold, functional-group type, lithium-salt environment, and first-shell topology. EMolPipe thereby organizes density-matrix predictions for chemical interpretation.



EMolAgent: Agent-Translated Design Space and Knowledge Copilot


EMolAgent is the interaction and physicochemical interpretation layer of EMolStudio. It translates a researcher’s natural-language question into a structured Agent-Translated Design Space by identifying candidate solvents, salt environments, target first-shell topologies, and requested electronic-structure readouts such as HOMO/LUMO, ESP, Li+–donor bond order, orbital localization, and Li+-centered ELF deformation. These structured definitions are dispatched to the integrated EMolConf–EMolES–EMolPipe workflow.


During execution, EMolAgent organizes automated molecular modeling, calls EMolES-i for density-matrix prediction and idempotency projection, and triggers electronic-structure postprocessing. The resulting physicochemical data are integrated into interactive views containing topology renderings, ESP surfaces, and energy-level comparisons, allowing researchers to evaluate key descriptors and adjust the design space.


EMolAgent also integrates a retrieval-augmented knowledge module linked to curated electrolyte-chemistry and computational-methodology resources. This module supports system-specific physical interpretation, parameter provenance, and follow-up analysis suggestions.

This lithium-salt environment is absent from the model training set. The frontier-orbital isosurface topology and fragment-component percentages reconstructed by EMolES-i agree with the DFT dominant-fragment assignments: the HOMO is mainly distributed on the DFTFB- fragment, with a contribution of 99.1%99.1\%, while the LUMO is mainly distributed on the FEC fragment, with a contribution of 96.7%96.7\%. This agreement supports fragment-resolved orbital analysis for this cluster.


We also follow Li+ ligand exchange along a two-stage coordination path in which an entering donor joins the first shell while a leaving donor departs (Supporting Information, Section S4). EMolES-i resolves the relative Li+ binding energy and accompanying Li–O bond-order evolution over the full 1000-frame path, using 30 DFT frames for validation. At those frames, the binding-energy mean absolute error is 0.084 eV (r=0.995r=0.995), compared with 0.380 eV for UMA under the same reference convention. The coupled energy and bond-order profiles place the strongest Li+ binding near transient coordination-shell closure and provide a continuous view between the DFT validation frames.

Electronic Effects of Molecular Functionalization


Using this workflow, we examine how molecular functionalization changes the electronic properties of an isolated electrolyte solvent before explicit solvation is introduced. This molecular view allows functional-group responses to be considered apart from the salt- and shell-dependent effects examined next. For each functionalized molecule, changes in the HOMO and LUMO energies, ESP extrema, dipole moment, and average Li+–donor bond order (BO) are reported relative to the corresponding parent scaffold under a consistent generation, relaxation, and analysis protocol (Supporting Information, Section S2).


Figure 4 summarizes these functionalization responses relative to the corresponding parent scaffolds. The single-site set contains 19,457 matched structures covering the Me, OMe, F, CF3, CO2Me, CN, SO2Me, and SO2F groups, and the multisite analysis follows one to four functionalized sites across 161,081 matched structures (Supporting Information, Section S1.1). Throughout this analysis, HOMO and LUMO energies in molecular level serve as redox-relevant frontier-orbital descriptors rather than as direct measures of the electrochemical window, which is further shaped by explicit coordination, reaction free energies, interfacial potential, and degradation pathways[45, 46, 47]. Likewise, ESPmin marks an electron-rich Lewis-basic pocket and ESPmax an electron-poor region of enhanced positive potential; together with solvating power, Li+ affinity, and local shell composition, these quantities constrain, but do not by themselves determine, solvation tendency[6, 7, 48].


Figure 4: Molecular electronic responses to functionalization. Values are changes relative to the corresponding parent scaffold. (a) Distributions of Δ\DeltaHOMO/Δ\DeltaLUMO, Δ\DeltaESPmax/Δ\DeltaESPmin, Δ\DeltaLi+–donor bond order, and Δ\Deltadipole moment for single-site functionalization over 19,457 matched samples; dots and bars mark medians and quantile ranges. (b) Me-referenced multiaxis comparison of frontier-orbital, ESP, dipole, and Li+–donor-contact modulation across CN, CF3, F, OMe, CO2Me, SO2Me, and SO2F. (c) Parent-conditioned Δ\DeltaESPmin and Δ\DeltaESPmax trends for all eight groups, colored as in (b). (d) Trajectories from one to four functionalized sites for CN, SO2Me, CO2Me, OMe, CF3, F, and Me; background colors indicate the single-site median direction and points trace the degree of functionalization.


The eight groups show distinct response patterns after single-site functionalization (Figure 4a,b; medians in Table S6). Me serves as an internal hydrocarbon reference, with near-zero median shifts in the frontier levels and the Li+–donor BO, and OMe provides a mild oxygenated reference that mainly adjusts the local oxygen environment and dipole moment. With Me as the reference, three broad patterns are apparent: stabilization of the low-lying unoccupied levels by CO2Me, CN, and the sulfonyl groups; HOMO stabilization by SO2F, CN, CF3, and F; and coupled changes in ESP, dipole moment, and Li+–donor contact for SO2Me and SO2F.


CO2Me and CN exemplify two distinct electron-accepting motifs. CO2Me shows a response consistent with carbonyl π∗\pi^{\ast} acceptor character and the largest LUMO stabilization upon single-site functionalization among the eight groups (median Δ\DeltaLUMO =−0.983=-0.983 eV), while its Li+–donor contact changes more moderately. CN combines the inductive withdrawal of the linear C≡\equivN unit with its large bond dipole, lowering both frontier levels (median Δ\DeltaHOMO/Δ\DeltaLUMO =−0.406/−0.636=-0.406/-0.636 eV), reinforcing the local positive field (Δ\DeltaESP=max+0.302{}_{\max}=+0.302 eV), and raising the dipole moment by +2.81+2.81 D. These molecular responses provide a reference for interpreting LUMO localization in explicit first shells, where Li+ coordination can reorganize solvent frontier orbitals and reduction-relevant state localization[49, 18].


CF3 and F display the inductive stabilization and local-field tuning characteristic of fluorination. Both functional groups lower the HOMO appreciably and raise ESPmax and ESPmin. CF3 shows larger local-field and Li+–donor-contact changes than a single F, and the scaffold-matched response planes of the Me/F/CF3 series show this graded fluorination trend (Supporting Information, Figure S7). These trends are consistent with the balance among fluorination degree, donor strength, and local coordination ability documented for fluorinated solvents and antisolvent/LHCE formulations[50, 51].


The sulfonyl groups show the largest combined changes in local electric field, dipole moment, and Li+–donor contact. SO2Me reorganizes the local potential around its polar sulfonyl unit, giving the largest median Δ\DeltaESPmax in the single-site set (+0.821+0.821 eV) together with the largest attenuation of the Li+–donor BO (−0.033-0.033). SO2F responds comparably in ESPmax (+0.808+0.808 eV) but adds deeper HOMO stabilization and the largest single-site dipole increase (+7.96+7.96 D). The lower BO is consistent with perturbation of the native Li+–donor environment alongside the increased polarity. This response is consistent with reported links among polar sulfone media, inner-shell structure, and interphase chemistry in sulfone-based and localized high-concentration electrolytes[52, 53, 12, 54].


The strength of these responses also depends on the electrostatic background of the parent scaffold (Figure 4c; Table S7). SO2Me, SO2F, CN, and CF3 amplify the local positive field most effectively on parents whose initial ESPmax is low, and the increment converges once the scaffold is already electron-poor; Δ\DeltaESPmin shifts analogously with the initial depth of the parent Lewis-basic pocket. Such scaffold–substituent coupling is consistent with classical Hammett-type substituent relationships and absolutely localized molecular orbital (ALMO) analyses, in which inductive effects, resonance, permanent electrostatics, and fragment-orbital mixing jointly set the frontier levels[55, 56]. A comparable interplay of scaffold and substituent has been reported in high-throughput surveys of organic optoelectronic molecules, where the two jointly delimit the accessible property window[57].


Following each group from one to four functionalized sites places these single-site effects on continuous trajectories (Figure 4d; endpoint values in Table S8, with the full depth-resolved distributions behind these medians in Figures S5 and S6). Me remains essentially flat across functionalization degrees, consistent with its use as the hydrocarbon reference. CO2Me deepens its LUMO stabilization from −0.983-0.983 to −1.537-1.537 eV while retaining a π∗\pi^{\ast}-dominated response and more modest changes in Li+–donor contact. CN shows one of the largest cumulative LUMO stabilizations in the set (−2.482-2.482 eV at four functionalized sites) alongside progressively deeper HOMO stabilization, and CF3 and F build up inductive stabilization with increasing fluorination. SO2Me shows increasingly coordinated changes in the ESP extrema, dipole moment, and Li+–donor contact, with its median BO response growing from −0.033-0.033 to −0.129-0.129. For most groups, the single-site response direction is retained at higher degrees of functionalization, while the increments attenuate. Single-site statistics summarize the response associated with each functional group, and multisite trajectories show how these responses accumulate, often sublinearly, within a scaffold.

Salt-Resolved Li+ First-Shell Chemistry


Molecular functionalization tunes the electronic properties of a candidate solvent, while its reactivity in an electrolyte also depends on the local environment formed around Li+ by solvent donors, salt anions, and diluents. Explicit first-shell clusters connect these levels: on the same relaxed structure, they allow us to follow which fragment hosts the frontier orbitals, how strongly Li+ maintains electronic contact with its donors, and how electronic environment around Li+ changes. Lithium-bond and lithium-ionic-bond pictures distinguish the electron-sharing and predominantly electrostatic components of Li+ coordination[8]. High-concentration and localized high-concentration electrolytes have highlighted anion entry into the first shell as an important factor in reaction pathways and interphase chemistry[9, 10, 12, 13], and solvent–anion charge-transfer studies show that fragment coupling can influence orbital energies and localization in multicomponent shells[58].


The cluster library comprises 22,500 explicit Li+-centered first-shell structures spanning LiPF6, LiFSI, LiDFOB, and LiTDI, with 5,625 structures per salt and 7,500 per coordination motif (Supporting Information, Section S1.2). The library includes three fixed motifs: solvent-rich M2X (two candidate-solvent molecules and one anion), diluent-containing MBX (one candidate solvent, one background solvent, and one anion), and anion-rich MX2 (one candidate solvent and two anions). For every structure, the projected density matrix provides the HOMO, LUMO, and gap, the ESP, the total Li+–donor bond order, the Li+-centered ELF deformation factor, and fragment-resolved frontier-orbital assignments (Section S2; full statistics in Tables S10–S14).


Figure 5: Salt-resolved frontier-orbital hosting and Li+-centered descriptors for the complete 22,500-cluster set. (a) HOMO and LUMO solvent-orbital share, defined as wsolvent/(wanion+wsolvent)×100%w_{\mathrm{solvent}}/(w_{\mathrm{anion}}+w_{\mathrm{solvent}})\times 100\%, for eight functional groups and four salts. The 0% and 100% limits denote anion- and solvent-dominated localization, respectively; points and density envelopes show distributions, and black dots mark means. (b) Distributions of total Li+–donor bond order and Li+-shell ELF deformation factor ϕ\phi for solvent-rich M2X, diluent-containing MBX, and anion-rich MX2 motifs; diamonds mark medians and the vertical reference in the ϕ\phi panels marks the pooled median.


Frontier-orbital hosting differs markedly among the four salts (Figure 5a; salt-pooled fractions in Table S10). LiPF6 clusters are dominated by solvent-derived frontier orbitals, with solvent-hosted fractions of 94.1% for the HOMO and 99.9% for the LUMO. LiTDI shows a contrasting occupied-state pattern: every one of its 5,625 HOMOs is anion-hosted, whereas 91.6% of its LUMOs remain solvent-hosted. LiFSI sits close to the HOMO partition boundary, with 46.6% solvent-hosted and 53.4% anion-hosted structures, alongside an almost completely solvent-hosted LUMO (99.9%), and LiDFOB pairs a predominantly anion-hosted HOMO (71.9%) with a predominantly solvent-hosted LUMO (71.1%). Together, these distributions capture solvent-derived frontier states, anion-derived occupied states, and mixed regimes across the four salts. These fractions describe the vertical frontier-orbital composition of the intact closed-shell cluster and do not by themselves set the reduction sequence. Anion-derived reduction is prominent in many concentrated and localized high-concentration electrolytes[9, 10, 12, 13]; for FSI- in particular, the favorable reduction reflects the relaxed reduced state and the dissociative reaction free energy of the anion rather than a low-lying vertical LUMO of the neutral shell[45, 46, 47]. The hosting statistics therefore indicate where reduction-relevant states reside, while their ordering requires reduced-state and reaction-pathway calculations.


The LiTDI pattern is consistent with recent work on self-compartmented LiTDI electrolytes: Ou et al. showed that TDI- enriches at the cathode interface, promotes coordinated anion-rich solvation structures, and raises the HOMO energy of the multi-anion motif Li+–4FSI-–1TDI- relative to free 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME) and other key solvation structures[59]. Within the first-shell library studied here, the TDI anion hosts the HOMO throughout, while most LUMOs are solvent-hosted and vary with functionalization.


Within the salts of mixed character, frontier-orbital localization also varies with molecular functionalization. For LiFSI, the solvent-hosted HOMO fraction ranges from 20.9% for CN to 71.3% for OMe, while the LUMO remains almost entirely solvent-hosted for all eight functional groups. For LiDFOB, LUMO hosting is strongly group-dependent: 97.9% of CN structures are solvent-hosted, compared with 0.4% for OMe and 0.9% for Me. LiTDI keeps an anion-hosted HOMO for every group, with Me and OMe LUMOs close to the solvent/anion boundary and the remaining classes predominantly solvent-hosted. Salt identity largely sets the dominant localization regime, while functionalization further modulates LUMO hosting within it. These localization patterns provide an electronic-structure perspective on the reported roles of DFOB-- and TDI--derived species in film formation, interphase construction, and anion-derived passivation[60, 61, 62, 63, 64, 65, 66, 67].


Total Li+–donor bond order condenses the aggregate electronic contact of the first shell into a single quantity (Figure 5b; Tables S10 and S11). The salt-pooled medians rank LiFSI (0.863) and LiDFOB (0.858) above LiPF6 (0.811), with LiTDI lower (0.698). Coordination topology has its largest effect for LiDFOB, whose median rises from 0.852 in M2X and 0.848 in MBX to 0.948 in anion-rich MX2. LiFSI reaches its highest median in the diluent-containing MBX motif (0.888), whereas LiTDI changes little across motifs (0.696–0.701). In this library, aggregate Li+–donor contact therefore varies primarily with salt identity and first-shell topology, with LiDFOB showing the largest response to anion-rich coordination. This ordering is consistent with the donor capacity of the anions themselves: the chelating oxalato oxygens of DFOB- add Li+ contacts as further anions enter the shell, whereas the charge-delocalized TDI- anion sustains the weakest aggregate contact.


The Li+-centered ELF deformation factor ϕ\phi varies over a narrower range: the salt-pooled medians span 1.0306–1.0323, and within each salt ϕ\phi shows no systematic relation to the total bond order (|r|≤0.19|r|\leq 0.19). Bond order and ELF deformation thus probe complementary aspects of first-shell chemistry: the integrated strength of Li+–environment electronic contact and the reorganization of electron localization around Li+. Functional-group effects on the total bond order are smaller than the salt and topology contrasts: SO2F gives the lowest pooled median (0.806), and the combined sulfonyl subset (median 0.814) sits below the remaining groups (0.832) (Table S13). Across this library, frontier-orbital placement varies more clearly with molecular functionalization, whereas Li+-centered contact is more strongly associated with salt identity and local topology.
